person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: method
span.quote: Offering a general and simple procedure for estimating and doing inference on θ0 that is formally valid in these highly complex settings is the main contribution of this paper.

span.label: regularization bias in semiparametric inference with machine-learned nuisance parameters
span.quote: We revisit the classic semiparametric problem of inference on a low dimensional parameter θ0 in the presence of high-dimensional nuisance parameters η0.

span.label: mathematical-proof
span.quote: In an appendix, we define additional notation and present proofs.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A TERM IS BORROWED PARTLY, FOR A PROCEDURE THE SOURCE USED DIFFERENTLY, AND THE INEXACT FIT IS STATED IN THE SAME SENTENCE: we use the term **CROSS-FITTING** to characterize our recommended procedure, **PARTLY BORROWING THE JARGON FROM** an earlier paper **WHICH EMPLOYED A SLIGHTLY DIFFERENT FORM** of sample-splitting. The word's provenance and its imprecision are both on the page
span.quote: We use the term “cross-fitting” to characterize our recommended procedure, partly borrowing the jargon from Fan et al. (2012) which employed a slightly different form of sample-splitting

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A TRADITIONAL ASSUMPTION IS SAID TO BREAK DOWN OUTSIDE ITS REGIME, AND THE REGIME IS NAMED: the paper departs from the classical setting BY ALLOWING the nuisance parameter to be SO HIGH-DIMENSIONAL that the traditional assumptions - **SUCH AS DONSKER PROPERTIES, THAT LIMIT COMPLEXITY OF THE PARAMETER SPACE** - **BREAK DOWN**. What fails is not a result but a condition, and the condition is named
span.quote: We depart from the classical setting by allowing for η0 to be so high-dimensional that the traditional assumptions, such as Donsker properties, that limit complexity of the parameter space for this object break down.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: TWO GOOD METHODS COMPOSED NAIVELY ARE SHOWN TO FAIL, AND THE WORD `NAIVELY` IS THE PAPER'S: both regularization bias and overfitting in estimating the nuisance parameter cause **A HEAVY BIAS** in estimators of the target that are obtained **BY NAIVELY PLUGGING** ML estimators into the estimating equations. Each piece is sound; the composition is not, and the paper names the fault in the composing rather than in either part
span.quote: However, both regularization bias and overfitting in estimating η0 cause a heavy bias in estimators of θ0 that are obtained by naively plugging ML estimators of η0 into estimating equations for θ0.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE REMEDY IS PRESENTED AS TWO INGREDIENTS AND THE RESULT IS GIVEN TWO NAMES AT ONCE: the impact can be removed using **TWO SIMPLE, YET CRITICAL, INGREDIENTS** - orthogonal moments with REDUCED SENSITIVITY to nuisance parameters, and cross-fitting - and **WE CALL THE RESULTING SET OF METHODS DOUBLE OR DEBIASED ML**. One method, two adjectives, offered as alternatives rather than ranked
span.quote: can be removed by using two simple, yet critical, ingredients: (1) using Neyman-orthogonal moments/scores that have reduced sensitivity with respect to nuisance parameters to estimate θ0, and (2) making use of cross-fitting which provides an efficient form of data-splitting. We call the resulting set of methods double or debiased ML (DML)

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A PROPERTY IS NAMED AFTER THE PERSON WHO INTRODUCED IT, AND THE ATTRIBUTION IS GIVEN AS THE REASON FOR THE NAME: we refer to property (1.8) as **NEYMAN ORTHOGONALITY** and to the score as the Neyman orthogonal score function **DUE TO THE FUNDAMENTAL CONTRIBUTIONS** in Neyman (1959) and Neyman (1979), **WHERE THIS NOTION WAS INTRODUCED**. The name records a debt, not a definition - and the property it names is a numbered equation, so the term is anchored to a formula rather than a gloss
span.quote: We refer to property (1.8) as “Neyman orthogonality” and to ψ as the Neyman orthogonal score function due to the fundamental contributions in Neyman (1959) and Neyman (1979), where this notion was introduced.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE FORMAL CONDITION IS GIVEN AN INTUITIVE GLOSS THAT STATES WHAT IT BUYS: **INTUITIVELY**, the orthogonality condition means the moment conditions used to identify the parameter are **LOCALLY INSENSITIVE** to the value of the nuisance parameter, **WHICH ALLOWS ONE TO PLUG IN NOISY ESTIMATES of these parameters WITHOUT STRONGLY VIOLATING the moment condition**. The gloss is not a restatement - it is the licence the condition grants
span.quote: Intuitively, the Neyman orthogonality condition means that the moment conditions used to identify θ0 are locally insensitive to the value of the nuisance parameter which allows one to plug-in noisy estimates of these parameters without strongly violating the moment condition.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A FUNCTION IS RENAMED WITH A HEDGING PREFIX WHEN ITS SPECIAL CASE IS GENERALISED: the criterion can be the log-likelihood associated to an observation - **MORE GENERALLY, WE REFER TO IT AS THE QUASI-LOG-LIKELIHOOD FUNCTION**. The prefix marks that the object no longer has the property its root name asserts
span.quote: can be the loglikelihood function associated to observation W . More generally, we refer to ℓ(W ; θ, β) as the quasi-log-likelihood function.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A CONDITION IS DECLARED NONPRIMITIVE AND ITS OWN CONDITIONS ARE DECLINED AS CASE-SPECIFIC: **THE ONLY NONPRIMITIVE CONDITION HERE** is the assumption on the rate of estimating the nuisance parameters - those rates are available for most used methods and are **CASE-SPECIFIC, SO WE DO NOT RESTATE** the conditions needed to reach them. The assumption is labelled as resting on assumptions that are not given
span.quote: The only nonprimitive condition here is the assumption on the rate of estimating the nuisance parameters. These rates of convergence are available for most often used ML methods and are case-specific, so we do not restate conditions that are needed to reach these rates.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A BOUND THE AUTHORS THEMSELVES IMPOSE IS NAMED **THE CRUDE BOUND**, AND FINER CONDITIONS ARE OFFERED IN ITS PLACE: a structural feature of the examples allows us to require **MUCH FINER CONDITIONS** on the quality of the nuisance parameter estimators **THAN THE CRUDE BOUND** (3.8). The paper's own requirement carries a pejorative as its standing name, and the numbered equation is what the pejorative attaches to
span.quote: This feature allows us to require much finer conditions on the quality of the nuisance parameter estimators than the crude bound (3.8).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A DISPENSED-WITH CONDITION IS REPLACED BY A WEAKER ONE AND THE REPLACEMENT IS THEN CRITICISED IN THE SAME PARAGRAPH: **WITHOUT INVOKING DONSKER CONDITIONS**, one may still show that the troublesome terms vanish **AS LONG AS** the entropy **DOES NOT INCREASE WITH N TOO RAPIDLY** - **HOWEVER, THESE CONDITIONS ON THE GROWTH OF ENTROPY COULD RESULT IN UNNECESSARILY STRONG RESTRICTIONS ON MODEL COMPLEXITY**. What was an assumption about a function class becomes a growth rate; the substitution is announced, and so is the price of the thing substituted in
span.quote: Without invoking Donsker conditions, one may still show that terms such as (1.7) vanish as long as GN ’s entropy does not increase with N too rapidly. A fairly general treatment is given in Belloni et al. (2017) who provide a set of conditions under which terms like c∗ can vanish making use of the full sample. However, these conditions on the growth of entropy could result in unnecessarily strong restrictions on model complexity

span.label: The regularity conditions given for the treatment-effect results are simplified rather than tightest possible
span.note: what this limits: the stated regularity conditions: THE CONDITIONS ARE NOT THE TIGHTEST POSSIBLE, BUT OFFER A SET OF SIMPLE CONDITIONS UNDER WHICH THEOREM 5.1 FOLLOWS AS A SPECIAL CASE
span.quote: The conditions are not the tightest possible, but offer a set of simple conditions under which Theorem 5.1 follows as a special case of the general theorem provided in Section 3.

span.label: Assumption 5.1 is simplified for presentation rather than stated at full sharpness
span.note: what this limits: Assumption 5.1 as stated: THE CONDITIONS ... ARE FAIRLY SHARP THOUGH SOMEWHAT SIMPLIFIED FOR EASE OF PRESENTATION
span.quote: The conditions in Assumption 5.1 are fairly sharp though somewhat simplified for ease of presentation.

span.label: The empirical finding that more folds gives smaller standard errors does not generalise
span.note: what this limits: any rule of thumb about cross-fitting folds: THERE DOES NOT APPEAR TO BE A GENERAL RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN THE NUMBER OF FOLDS IN CROSS-FITTING AND THE PRECISION OF THE ESTIMATE OF THE PARAMETER OF INTEREST
span.quote: While intuitive, we note that this statement does not seem to be generalizable in that there does not appear to be a general relationship between the number of folds in cross-fitting and the precision of the estimate of the parameter of interest; see the next example.

span.label: Deep-learning nuisance estimators were tried but hit stability and computational problems and were left unreported
span.note: what this limits: the set of nuisance estimators the empirical section reports: deep learning was tried, and WE RAN INTO STABILITY AND COMPUTATIONAL ISSUES AND CHOSE NOT TO REPORT THESE RESULTS IN THE EMPIRICAL SECTION
span.quote: However, we ran into stability and computational issues and chose not to report these results in the empirical section.

span.label: The rate condition the method is known for is a crude bound that follows only under one of the paper's conditions.
span.note: what this limits: the o(N^-1/4) nuisance rate usually quoted from this paper: the authors state it is the crude requirement imposed if only condition (3.7) holds, and that the conditions can be refined
span.quote: If only (3.7) holds, Assumption 3.2, particularly λ′ N = o(N −1/2), imposes the (crude) rate requirement

span.label: Several of the paper's own headline applications admit weaker conditions than the crude one.
span.note: what this limits: any application of the crude rate requirement: the authors note that many important structured problems - including partially linear regression models and average treatment effects under unconfoundedness - have vanishing cross-derivatives and so allow more refined requirements
span.quote: We note that many important structured problems – such as estimation of parameters in partially linear regression models, estimation of parameters in partially linear structural equation models, and estimation of average treatment effects under unconfoundedness – are such that some cross-derivatives vanish

span.label: Identification is assumed, not established: it is listed among the conditions the theorems require.
span.note: what this limits: the causal interpretation of estimates from this method: the identification condition is imposed as an assumption alongside Neyman orthogonality and smoothness, so the theory delivers estimation and inference for a parameter that is already identified
span.quote: The identification condition holds; namely, the singular values of the matrix are between c0 and c1. J0 := EP [ψa(W ; η0)] Assumption 3.1 requires scores to be Neyman orthogonal or near-orthogonal and imposes mild smoothness requirements as well as the canonical identification condition

span.label: The insensitivity to the nuisance estimate is local and approximate, in the authors' own gloss.
span.note: what this limits: the claim that this method is robust to the choice of nuisance estimator: the moment conditions are described as locally insensitive to the nuisance value, permitting noisy plug-in estimates without strongly violating the moment condition
span.quote: Intuitively, the Neyman orthogonality condition means that the moment conditions used to identify θ0 are locally insensitive to the value of the nuisance parameter which allows one to plug-in noisy estimates of these parameters without strongly violating the moment condition

span.label: flexibly controlling for a rich set of variables in the 401(k) example, where assignment is observational - and the elimination holds only under the paper's own identifying assumptions, which the sentence states as an aim rather than a demonstrated result
span.quote: In this example, the treatment variable is not randomly assigned and we aim to eliminate the potential biases due to the lack of random assignment by flexibly controlling for a rich set of variables.

span.label: Neyman-orthogonal moments/scores → regularization bias
span.note: the method REMOVES the impact of a bias that the naive estimator suffers - the paper's own central result, stated as a repair rather than a relation between two objects of study
span.quote: We show that the impact of regularization bias and overfitting on estimation of the parameter of interest θ0 can be removed by using two simple, yet critical, ingredients: (1) using Neyman-orthogonal moments/scores that have reduced sensitivity with respect to nuisance parameters

span.label: the o(N^-1/4) rate - A WORST CASE, NOT THE REQUIREMENT: the paper calls it the crude requirement that smooth problems translate to, and says in the same breath that the conditions can be refined, so the number that travels out of this paper is the loosest form of a condition the paper itself tightens
span.quote: In smooth problems, these conditions translate to the crude requirement that nuisance parameters are estimated at the o(N −1/4) rate as discussed previously in the case with linear scores. However, these conditions can be refined

span.label: Neyman orthogonality - A DERIVATIVE AT A POINT, GLOSSED AS LOCAL INSENSITIVITY: the moment condition is locally insensitive to the nuisance value, which is what licenses plugging in noisy estimates without strongly violating it; the property is evaluated at the truth and both hedges - locally, and without strongly violating - are in the sentence that explains it
span.quote: Intuitively, the Neyman orthogonality condition means that the moment conditions used to identify θ0 are locally insensitive to the value of the nuisance parameter which allows one to plug-in noisy estimates of these parameters without strongly violating the moment condition

span.label: cross-fitting - COINED IN THIS SENTENCE, WITH ITS DEFINITION ATTACHED: the name is introduced for the procedure of swapping the roles of main and auxiliary samples and averaging the resulting estimates, so unlike the eponyms in our absent-names table this word cannot come apart from its referent - the paper that named it also defined it
span.quote: We call this sample splitting procedure where we swap the roles of main and auxiliary samples to obtain multiple estimates and then average the results cross-fitting
